scripts.title: Getting through the egg case
scripts.reason: Strongest link between an unusual biological mechanism and a concrete inspection lesson.
scripts.text:
Why would a wasp lay its egg inside a cockroach’s egg case?

An ensign wasp puts her egg there because the cockroach eggs will feed her young.

She braces herself against the case and pushes in the thin tube she uses to lay eggs. Getting through that tough outer wall usually takes 15 to 30 minutes.

She leaves one egg inside. When it hatches, the young wasp uses tiny jaws with small teeth to cut into the cockroach eggs around it.

American cockroaches leave their egg cases in small cracks and gaps. So when you check those warm, damp hiding places, look for egg cases as well as live roaches.

scripts.title: Recognizing the wasp
scripts.reason: Useful identification details explain the visitor and lead to a practical inspection step.
scripts.text:
Why would a wasp lay its egg inside a cockroach’s egg case?

That's an ensign wasp. Her young feeds on the cockroach eggs inside.

It gets its name from the little flag-shaped part at the back of its body. That part sits on a thin stalk and bobs up and down.

The adult is only about five to seven millimeters long, and it doesn't sting or bite people.

If you find one indoors, you can check for roaches with sticky traps. These catch roaches on a layer of glue as they walk across.

Place them against walls under sinks or behind appliances. Use what they catch to guide your roach inspection, and leave the harmless wasp alone.

scripts.title: From egg to adult, inside the case
scripts.reason: A coherent visual story follows the wasp through feeding, pupation and emergence.
scripts.text:
Why would a wasp lay its egg inside a cockroach’s egg case?

The cockroach eggs feed a young ensign wasp, but the case also holds it while it grows into an adult.

The mother places one egg inside. When that wasp egg hatches, the young wasp uses pointed jaws with tiny teeth to cut into the cockroach eggs around it.

After feeding and growing, the young wasp changes into an adult right there inside the egg case.

When it's ready to leave, the adult wasp cuts a small opening through the outer case and comes out.

scripts.title: Finding where roaches are active
scripts.reason: Specific trap-placement advice explains where to monitor and how catches guide inspection.
scripts.text:
Why would a wasp lay its egg inside a cockroach’s egg case?

An ensign wasp lays her egg there so her young can feed on the cockroach eggs.

If you see one indoors and want to check for roaches, use sticky traps. They catch roaches on a layer of glue as the insects walk across.

Roaches tend to follow walls and edges. Put the traps right against a wall, under a sink or behind the refrigerator.

A trap beside an outside door can also help you check for roaches coming in from outdoors.

Put traps in a few different places and check them regularly. Start a closer inspection where you're catching the most roaches.

scripts.title: Checking for roaches and their eggs
scripts.reason: Brief egg-case comparison and packing advice add practical prevention value, with a looser connection to the wasp story.
scripts.text:
Why would a wasp lay its egg inside a cockroach’s egg case?

An ensign wasp lays one egg inside, and her young feeds on the cockroach eggs. American cockroach egg cases are one of her targets.

American roaches leave their egg cases in small cracks and gaps. Female German roaches carry theirs until the eggs are ready to hatch.

Cardboard boxes can hide roaches and their egg cases, so clear away boxes you don't need after unpacking.

Before bringing bags, boxes or luggage indoors, check for both live roaches and their egg cases.
